passage: Avni's phone buzzed again during the maths lesson. The class game group was laughing at a voice message she had sent the night before. Someone had looped it, with jokes underneath. “Squeaky Avni,” one wrote. Ujjwal, who sat behind her, had typed a laugh at first, then nothing. Avni could not leave the group: that was where the plans for the match were made, and leaving meant losing everyone. She had not told anyone at home, in case Papa took the phone away. That evening Papa found her in the corridor, eyes red. She showed him, hands shaking. He sat on the floor next to her. “Thank you for telling me. This isn't your fault, and nobody's taking your phone.” He saved the messages and emailed the class teacher that night. The reply came before breakfast: thank you for telling me; the clip comes down today, and I will speak to the group this morning.

qa.q: Why could Avni not leave the class game group?
qa.a: The plans for the match were made in the group, and leaving meant losing everyone.

qa.q: Why had Avni not told anyone at home?
qa.a: Avni was afraid that Papa would take the phone away, and probably felt ashamed and trapped.

qa.q: What did Papa do the same evening that helped?
qa.a: Papa sat beside her, thanked her for telling him, said it was not her fault and that the phone would stay, then saved the messages and emailed the class teacher that night.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have been feeling after typing a laugh at first and then nothing?
qa.a: Ujjwal may have felt uneasy or guilty about joining in, unsure how to stop it, which fits going quiet.

grounding: A teenager mocked in a group chat feels trapped, since leaving means losing the group and she fears losing her device, and an adult at home responds the same day.

passage:
“Why are you always in the bathroom with your phone?” asked Lakshmi's older sister Trisha, leaning on the door.
“No reason.”
“Lakshmi.”
Lakshmi's voice came out small. “There's a lobby for the game. Some of them make jokes about me every time I play, and others just laugh. If I leave, I lose all my teammates.”
“Since when?”
“Three weeks. Don't tell Mummy, she'll take the phone.”
Trisha sat on the floor beside her. “It's not your fault. I won't tell behind your back. Come with me and we'll tell her together, and I'll ask her to let you keep the phone.”
That evening Mummy listened without interrupting. “Thank you for telling me. Let's save these messages, block them and report the lobby right now, together.”

qa.q: How long had the jokes been going on?
qa.a: The jokes had been going on for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say, “Don't tell Mummy, she'll take the phone”?
qa.a: Lakshmi was afraid of losing the phone and the teammates, and felt trapped between the harassment and the fear of a punishment.

qa.q: What did Trisha choose to do instead of telling Mummy behind Lakshmi's back?
qa.a: Trisha sat beside Lakshmi, said it was not her fault and offered to go together to tell Mummy and ask her to let Lakshmi keep the phone.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt while listening without interrupting?
qa.a: Mummy was probably worried and concerned, but kept calm so that Lakshmi could finish, which shows in thanking Lakshmi for telling.

grounding: A teenager who is mocked in a game lobby feels trapped, hides it for fear of losing her device, and an older sister and Mummy respond the same day.

passage: Lalit, thanks for having me on the school radio. So, last year, in our gaming group, the others started calling me 'the potato' every time I lost. Then they made edits of my face and posted them in the group chat, and everyone laughed. I couldn't leave; those were my only friends after school. And I didn't tell my parents, because I was sure they'd take my phone. One night I just stopped eating dinner. My mother noticed and sat with me on the stairs. I told her. She didn't take the phone. She read the chats with me, helped me screenshot everything, and that same night she messaged my class teacher. The next day the school called the other boys' parents, and the edits were deleted. I'm Anirban, and I'm saying this because you won't lose your phone for telling.

qa.q: What did the group call Anirban after a loss?
qa.a: 'The potato'.

qa.q: Why didn't Anirban tell anyone at home at first?
qa.a: Anirban felt trapped and scared, sure the phone would be taken away, and the group were Anirban's only after-school friends.

qa.q: What did Anirban's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She listened on the stairs, didn't take the phone, helped screenshot everything and messaged the class teacher that same night.

qa.q: What was it like for Anirban's mother to notice the skipped dinner?
qa.a: She was probably worried and alert, which is why she sat on the stairs with Anirban and acted the same night.

grounding: A teenager mocked in a gaming group feels trapped and hides it for fear of losing his phone, until his mother responds the same night.

passage: Monday: in the class group chat, someone posted a photo of Lavanya's old school bag with the caption 'beggar style'. Eighteen laughing replies. Lavanya typed 'lol' so no one would think she minded, then cried in the bathroom. Wednesday: the jokes kept coming. She thought of leaving the group, but then she'd miss every class update and look even more like a loser. She didn't tell Amma; the last time there was trouble, Amma took the phone for a month. At lunch she finally showed Jahnavi. Jahnavi said, 'This is bullying. Come on,' and walked her straight to Mrs Fernandes, their class teacher, that afternoon. Mrs Fernandes screenshotted everything, called Lavanya's mother herself before four, and told her the phone wasn't the problem. The next Monday: the class had a new chat, with the teacher in it, and the photo was gone.

qa.q: What caption was posted with Lavanya's school bag?
qa.a: 'Beggar style'.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya type 'lol'?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and trapped, and wanted no one to see how hurt she was; then she cried in the bathroom.

qa.q: What made Jahnavi's response strong?
qa.a: She named it as bullying and took Lavanya to the class teacher the same afternoon, instead of just sympathising.

qa.q: How might Amma feel after Mrs Fernandes's call?
qa.a: Likely worried and upset for Lavanya, and helped by hearing the phone wasn't the problem, so she can support rather than punish.

grounding: Over a week a teenager mocked in a class chat feels trapped and hides it from home, until a friend takes her to a teacher who acts that day.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage: Sarika, you think nobody understands what happens in those game chats? Your Indu mami taught school for thirty years; sit. About ten years ago, a boy in my class, Farooq, started coming in with red eyes. In his online game, a group of older players kept calling him names and kicking him out of matches the moment he joined. He didn't quit, because his only friends from his old town played there. And he didn't tell his father, because he was sure he'd lose the computer. One afternoon I kept him back after class and asked. He broke down. I told him it wasn't his fault, and that same evening his father and I sat with him, reported the accounts and set up a new private team with his real friends. His father didn't take the computer. Farooq told me later that was the part he remembered most.

qa.q: How long did Indu mami teach school?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: Why did Farooq keep playing despite the name-calling?
qa.a: He felt trapped, because his only friends from his old town played there, and afraid of losing the computer if he told.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Farooq most, and why?
qa.a: Indu asking him privately and then, the same evening, sitting with his father to report the accounts without taking the computer, so he felt safe telling.

qa.q: What might Farooq's father have felt on learning about it?
qa.a: Likely shocked and protective, and his choice not to take the computer showed Farooq he wasn't being punished.

grounding: A retired teacher recalls a boy harassed in an online game who hid it for fear of losing his computer, and the same-day help he got.

passage: Anand's squad in the evening game had turned. For two weeks, whenever he logged in, the lobby filled with voice lines: "Noob's here," "Mute the baby," a nickname about his cracking voice. He could leave, but the squad was also his whole class section; leaving meant eating lunch alone too. With board exams a month away, he told himself it didn't matter and kept playing past midnight, jaw tight. He didn't tell Papa, who had already threatened to lock the tablet away until exams. On Friday his didi, Parul, home from her office, saw him flinch at the screen. "What's going on?" It came out in a rush. Parul didn't grab the tablet. She sat with him, then went straight to Papa. That same evening Papa listened and said, "This isn't your fault, and I won't take the tablet for telling me." Together they reported the players and wrote to his class teacher.

qa.q: What had Papa threatened to do?
qa.a: Papa had threatened to lock the tablet away until exams.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep the mocking from Papa?
qa.a: He was afraid of losing the tablet and felt trapped, because leaving the game meant losing his classmates too.

qa.q: How did Parul and Papa respond well once Anand spoke up?
qa.a: Parul listened without grabbing the tablet and went to Papa at once; that evening Papa reassured Anand, kept the device with him, reported the players and wrote to the teacher.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt seeing her brother flinch at the screen?
qa.a: She was probably worried and protective, sensing something was wrong behind his tight jaw.

grounding: Shows a teenager mocked in a game lobby who feels trapped and hides it for fear of losing his device, until family respond the same day.
